newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan appetite for sterling bonds seen continuing.
newsitem.headline: Japan appetite for sterling bonds seen continuing.

text.p: Japanese brokerages are expected to keep feeding sterling-based bonds to domestic retail investors as Britain's general election has not altered the interest rate trend there, underwriters said on Tuesday.
They said that while issuance of such bonds had fallen slightly from peaks earlier in the year, demand from yield-hungry Japanese investors have remained solid.

"We saw the pound lose ground after the election, but that has not lasted long. With British interest rates staying around current levels, we are not planning to change our plans for now," a manager at a major securities firm said.

On Friday, sterling fell temporary across board, partly in reaction to a column in a British newspaper suggesting that the Labour Party would have to adopt policies to gradually drive down the pound to avoid economic damage to the country.
The manager at the securities firm said that as long as yields on sterling-based bonds remained attractive, the appetite of Japanese investors should continue.
"The brief fall of the pound after the election has not frightened investors," he said.
Last month, Japan's Nikko Securities Co Ltd lead-managed 150 million pounds worth of 6.3 percent Euronotes issued by Austria's Oesterreichische Kontrollbank.
Earlier in April, Nomura Securities Co Ltd acted as lead manager for a sterling issuance by Canada's Export Development Corp and another by Oesterreichische Kontrollbank.
A manager at Nomura's global capital group said that it had lead-managed a total of about 1.1 billion pounds of sterling-based bonds since the start of the year.
The underwriting sources said that Tony Blair's election victory in Britain had been widely expected by the market.
"The thought of a soft pound shocked the market for a moment, but I think it's premature to speculate on the new government's policy at this stage," an underwriting source at another brokerage said.

"I don't expect the new government's policy to change dramatically from that of the previous one, so I don't think there is any immediate worry about Japanese investors withdrawing funds from sterling," the source said.
